title: Predicate: test, and, or, negate
description: Create Predicates to test whether a number is even and whether it is greater than 5. Use and(), or(), and negate() to build compound predicates. Test each against several integers and print results.
hints: isEven.and(greaterThan5) returns a new Predicate that is true only when both are true.
isEven.negate() returns a Predicate that inverts the result.

solution.explanation: Predicate<T> is a functional interface in java.util.function with a single abstract method boolean test(T t). The default methods and(Predicate), or(Predicate), and negate() return new composed Predicates — they implement short-circuit evaluation just like && and ||: and() skips the second predicate if the first returns false, and or() skips the second if the first returns true. This composability lets you build arbitrarily complex filters from simple, reusable primitives without any if-else chains.

Returns a composed predicate representing logical AND; short-circuits if this returns false.
Returns a composed predicate representing logical OR; short-circuits if this returns true.

title: Predicate.isEqual and Chaining in a Filter
description: Use Predicate.isEqual() to create a predicate that matches a specific string. Then write a generic filterList method that takes a List<T> and a Predicate<T> and returns a new list of matching elements. Demonstrate with string length and equality filters.
hints: Predicate.isEqual("apple") returns a Predicate<Object> that tests equals.
Chain predicates: startsWithA.and(longerThan5) for compound filters.

solution.explanation: Predicate.isEqual(target) is a static factory method that returns a Predicate equivalent to Objects.equals(target, t) — it handles null safely (Predicate.isEqual(null).test(null) returns true). The generic filterList method demonstrates how Predicates integrate naturally with regular Java code before you learn streams — it's essentially implementing Stream.filter manually. The chaining pattern (and/or) lets you compose complex queries from simple building blocks, making the intent of each filter clear and the predicates reusable across different call sites.

title: Function: apply, andThen, compose, identity
description: Create Functions for: (1) converting a String to its length, (2) doubling an integer, (3) converting an integer to its hex string. Use andThen to chain them: String -> length -> doubled. Use compose for the reverse pipeline. Use Function.identity() as a no-op.
hints: f.andThen(g) means: apply f first, then pass the result to g.
f.compose(g) means: apply g first, then pass the result to f.

solution.explanation: Function<T,R> represents a function from T to R. apply(T t) evaluates it. andThen(Function<R,V> after) creates a composed function that applies this first and passes the result to after — it's left-to-right composition (the more readable direction). compose(Function<V,T> before) creates a composed function that applies before first, then this — it's right-to-left composition like mathematical function composition. Function.identity() returns a function that always returns its input argument, useful as a neutral element in functional pipelines or as a placeholder. andThen chains are compile-time checked: each step's output type must match the next step's input type.

title: Function<String, Integer> for Parsing and Transformation Pipeline
description: Build a data transformation pipeline using Functions. Parse a list of CSV strings like "Alice,30,Engineer" into Person objects. Chain: csvString -> String[] -> Person. Print each Person.
hints: splitCsv = line -> line.split(",");
Chain: splitCsv.andThen(toPerson) gives Function<String, Person>.

solution.explanation: Composing small, single-purpose Functions into a pipeline is a key functional programming pattern. Each function does one thing: splitCsv only splits, toPerson only constructs. andThen chains them into a single Function<String, Person> that is reusable and easily testable in isolation. This design also makes it trivial to insert a new transformation step (e.g., a trimming function) between existing steps without modifying either. In production code, these small functions often replace verbose static utility methods and are passed to Stream.map() to process collections.

title: Consumer: accept and andThen
description: Create a Consumer<String> that prints a string in uppercase and another that prints its length. Use andThen to chain them so both actions happen on each input. Apply to a list of words.
hints: printUpper.andThen(printLength) returns a new Consumer that does both in sequence.
Use a for-each loop and call the combined consumer's accept() method.

solution.explanation: Consumer<T> is a functional interface whose accept(T t) method performs an action on T but returns nothing (void). It is used for side effects like printing, logging, or updating state. andThen(Consumer<? super T> after) returns a new Consumer that performs this consumer's action first and then after's action on the same input — unlike Function.andThen, there's no chaining of return values since Consumers return void. This is commonly seen in forEach calls: list.forEach(printUpper.andThen(printLength)) applies both actions to every element.

methodSignatures.description: Performs this operation on the given argument.
Returns a composed Consumer that performs this operation first, then after.

title: BiConsumer: accept with Two Arguments
description: Create a BiConsumer<String, Integer> that prints a name with a score. Use it to iterate a Map<String, Integer> of student scores with forEach. Then chain two BiConsumers with andThen.
hints: Map.forEach(BiConsumer<K,V>) calls the BiConsumer for each entry.
printScore.andThen(printGrade) chains both consumers on each key-value pair.

solution.explanation: BiConsumer<T,U> accepts two arguments and returns nothing — it's the two-argument version of Consumer. Map.forEach(BiConsumer<K,V>) passes each key-value pair to the BiConsumer, making it the cleanest way to iterate a map when you need both the key and value. BiConsumer also has andThen, allowing you to chain multiple operations on the same pair of arguments. BiConsumer is also used in Map.replaceAll (BiFunction variant), Map.compute, and when building event handlers that need two pieces of context.

title: Supplier: get and Lazy Initialization
description: Create a Supplier<List<String>> that lazily creates and populates a list only when get() is called. Then demonstrate a lazy initialization pattern: only compute an expensive value if it's needed.
hints: Supplier<T> has a single method T get() with no arguments.
For lazy init: if (cachedValue == null) { cachedValue = expensiveSupplier.get(); }

solution.explanation: Supplier<T> is a functional interface with a single abstract method T get() that takes no arguments and returns a value. Unlike a direct field assignment, a Supplier defers execution until get() is called — this is lazy evaluation. The lazy initialization pattern (check null, then call supplier) is the non-thread-safe version of the double-checked locking idiom; for thread safety you'd use AtomicReference or a synchronized block. Suppliers are used extensively in the JDK: Optional.orElseGet(Supplier), Objects.requireNonNullElseGet, and logging frameworks that accept message suppliers to avoid string concatenation when logging is disabled.

methodSignatures.description: Gets a result. Each call may or may not return the same object depending on the implementation.

title: Supplier Memoization Pattern
description: Implement a memoize(Supplier<T>) utility that wraps a Supplier so the value is computed only once and cached for subsequent calls. Demonstrate that the expensive computation runs exactly once.
hints: Use an array or AtomicReference to hold the cached value within the closure.
Boolean flag or null-check: if not computed yet, call supplier.get() and store the result.

solution.explanation: Memoization caches the result of a function so it is computed only once regardless of how many times get() is called. The implementation uses a single-element Object array and boolean array rather than local variables because lambdas in Java can only close over effectively final variables — arrays are effectively final (the reference doesn't change) even though their contents can be mutated. The returned lambda is a closure that captures both arrays and the original supplier. Note this implementation is not thread-safe; for thread safety use AtomicReference and compare-and-set, or use synchronized.

methodSignatures.description: Returns a Supplier that computes the value once on first call and caches it for subsequent calls.

title: BiFunction: apply and andThen
description: Create a BiFunction<String, Integer, String> that repeats a string n times. Use andThen to transform the result. Also create a BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> for addition and use it with a list of pairs.
hints: BiFunction<T,U,R>.apply(T t, U u) takes two arguments and returns R.
andThen(Function<R,V> after) composes a function on the result of BiFunction.

solution.explanation: BiFunction<T,U,R> is the two-argument version of Function<T,R>: apply(T t, U u) takes two inputs and returns one output. andThen(Function<R,V> after) composes a unary Function on the result — note that BiFunction does not have compose() because there is no clean way to compose two functions before a two-input function. BiFunction is used throughout the JDK: Map.merge, Map.compute, Map.replaceAll all accept BiFunction variants. The repeat(String, int) pattern also shows how BiFunction cleanly replaces a static utility method in a composable, passable form.

title: UnaryOperator and BinaryOperator
description: Use UnaryOperator<String> to transform strings (trim then capitalize). Use BinaryOperator<Integer> to find the max of two integers. Apply UnaryOperator with List.replaceAll and BinaryOperator with Stream.reduce.
hints: UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T> — the input and output are the same type.
Use list.replaceAll(unaryOp) and stream.reduce(BinaryOperator) for practical application.

solution.explanation: UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T> — it specializes Function for the case where input and output are the same type, making the intent clearer. List.replaceAll(UnaryOperator<E>) applies the operator to each element in-place, replacing each element with the operator's result. BinaryOperator<T> extends BiFunction<T,T,T> — both inputs and the output are the same type. Stream.reduce(BinaryOperator<T>) repeatedly applies the operator to combine all elements into a single result; without an identity element it returns Optional<T> because the stream might be empty. Integer::max and Math::max are commonly used as BinaryOperators.

methodSignatures.description: Replaces each element in the list with the result of applying the operator.
Reduces the stream elements using an associative accumulation function, returning an Optional.

title: Static Method References
description: Replace lambda expressions with static method references for: Math::abs on a list of integers, Integer::parseInt on a list of strings, and Integer::toBinaryString. Print results for each.
hints: Math::abs is ClassName::staticMethod — equivalent to n -> Math.abs(n).
Integer::parseInt is equivalent to s -> Integer.parseInt(s).

solution.explanation: A static method reference has the form ClassName::staticMethodName and is equivalent to a lambda that calls that static method with the lambda's argument. The compiler matches the method reference to the target functional interface by checking that the method's parameter and return types match the interface's abstract method signature. Math::abs matches Function<Integer,Integer> because it takes one Integer and returns one Integer. Static method references are the most straightforward kind — the class name is fixed, and the argument is passed directly to the static method.

title: Instance Method References (Unbound and Bound)
description: Demonstrate the two kinds of instance method references: (1) Unbound: String::toUpperCase, String::length used as Function<String, String> and Function<String, Integer>. (2) Bound: a specific String instance's method: str::contains used as Predicate<String>.
hints: Unbound: String::toUpperCase is equiv to s -> s.toUpperCase(). The string itself is the first arg.
Bound: prefix::contains is equiv to s -> prefix.contains(s). The specific object is captured.

solution.explanation: There are two kinds of instance method references. An unbound reference (String::toUpperCase) refers to an instance method of a specific class but the receiver object is supplied as the first argument at call time — so it fits Function<String,String> where the String argument becomes the 'this' of the method. A bound reference (substring::contains) captures a specific object instance (substring) and the lambda's argument becomes the method's parameter — so it fits Predicate<String> where the String argument is passed to contains(). The difference is subtle: String::toUpperCase means 'call toUpperCase on whatever String is given'; substring::contains means 'call contains on this specific String, passing the given argument'.

methodSignatures.description: Returns this string converted to upper case.
Returns true if this string contains the specified sequence of char values.

title: Constructor References
description: Use constructor references (ClassName::new) to create objects. Demonstrate with ArrayList::new as a Supplier, String::new as a Function<char[],String>, and a custom Person class constructor reference used as a BiFunction.
hints: ArrayList::new as Supplier<List<String>> calls the no-arg constructor.
Person::new as BiFunction<String,Integer,Person> calls the two-arg constructor.

solution.explanation: Constructor references (ClassName::new) work like method references but invoke a constructor. The compiler selects the constructor overload that matches the target functional interface's abstract method signature — Supplier<T> maps to the no-arg constructor, Function<A,T> maps to the one-arg constructor, BiFunction<A,B,T> maps to the two-arg constructor. Constructor references are often used in conjunction with streams (stream.map(Person::new)) or as factory arguments. Each call to the supplier/function creates a new, independent object, which is why list1 and list2 are separate lists despite using the same factory.

title: Building a Reusable Validator with Predicates
description: Build a Validator<T> class that chains multiple Predicates and collects error messages for those that fail. Use it to validate a user registration object (username length, email format, age range).
hints: Store each rule as a pair of (Predicate<T>, String errorMessage) in a list.
validate() iterates all rules; if predicate.test(value) is false, add the error message.

solution.explanation: The Validator pattern separates rule definition from rule execution, making rules independently testable and easily extensible without modifying the Validator class. Each rule stores both a Predicate (the test logic) and an error message (the failure feedback), treating them as a single logical unit. The builder-style addRule(...) that returns this allows method chaining, creating a fluent API that reads like a specification. The validate method collects all failures rather than stopping at the first, giving the caller a complete picture — this is preferable in UI validation scenarios where users need to see all errors at once.

methodSignatures.description: Adds a validation rule; returns this for method chaining.
Runs all rules against the value and returns a list of error messages for failed rules.

title: BinaryOperator in Reduce and Accumulation
description: Use BinaryOperator to implement: (1) a running product of a list of integers, (2) string concatenation with a separator using reduce, (3) finding the longest string in a list. Use both the identity-based and no-identity reduce overloads.
hints: reduce(identity, BinaryOperator) never returns Optional; reduce(BinaryOperator) returns Optional.
For the longest string: (a, b) -> a.length() >= b.length() ? a : b

solution.explanation: Stream.reduce has two overloads: reduce(T identity, BinaryOperator<T>) uses an identity value (like 0 for sum, 1 for product) that is used as the initial accumulator and also defines the result when the stream is empty — it always returns T. reduce(BinaryOperator<T>) has no identity and therefore returns Optional<T> because the stream might be empty and there would be no value to return. BinaryOperator<T> extends BiFunction<T,T,T>, so both inputs and the output are the same type T — this is required for the associative accumulation pattern that allows parallel reduction. String joining is better done with Collectors.joining in production, but this illustrates the reduce mechanics.

methodSignatures.description: Reduces the stream using the identity value and associative accumulation function.
Reduces the stream using the accumulation function; returns empty Optional if the stream is empty.

title: Composing a Processing Pipeline with Function
description: Build a text processing pipeline using Function composition. Steps: (1) trim whitespace, (2) convert to lowercase, (3) remove punctuation, (4) split into words, (5) count word frequency. Compose steps 1-3 as a single Function<String,String>, then apply steps 4-5.
hints: trim.andThen(lower).andThen(removePunctuation) creates a single Function<String,String>.
After cleaning, split on '\\s+' and count with a HashMap.

solution.explanation: Function composition with andThen creates a pipeline where each function's output feeds into the next function's input, all resolved at compile time. This approach separates each transformation step into a named, testable function — if the logic changes (e.g., different punctuation rules), only one function needs to be updated. Using method references (String::trim, String::toLowerCase) where possible makes the pipeline self-documenting. The entire clean pipeline is just one line to apply, hiding the multi-step complexity behind a simple clean.apply(text) call — this is the core value of functional composition.
